newsitem.title: USA: Fosamax, taxol show cancer-fighting promise - study.
newsitem.headline: Fosamax, taxol show cancer-fighting promise - study.

text.p: A combination of Merck and Co's osteoporosis treatment Fosomax with taxol showed promise in preventing the spread of cancer to the bone, a new study showed.

In a study published in the May issue of "Invasion and Metastases", Mark Stearns, professor of pathology and laboratory medicine at Allegheny University of Health Sciences, set out to determine if fortifying the bone using Fosamax would block bone metastases altogether.
Fosomax, or alendronate, is used to treat osteoporosis in post-menopausal women and for the treatment of bone disorder Paget's disease.

Stearns found while Fosamax alone did block bone metastases, it did not protect the soft tissue from cancer, Steans said. By using taxol with Fosamax, Stearns said he could protect the bone with Fosamax and the tissue with taxol.

Taxol, derived from the yew tree, has been used successfully in patients with malignant melanoma, breast and ovarian cancer, and has been partially effective in delaying the progress of prostate cancer bone metastases in patients, Stearns said.
He said both Fosamax and taxol both inhibited MMP-2, a substance overproduced by prostate cancer tumors, suggesting MMP-2 might be a key target of the two drugs.

"The spread of cancer to the bone probably involves bone resorption," Stearns said. "Fosamax is potent inhibitor of bone reabsorption and might therefore directly affect tumor cell establishment, attachment and survival in the bone/bone marrow environment."
